pharm: Broad-spectrum benzimidazole anthelmintic that binds parasite beta-tubulin and disrupts microtubule formation, impairing glucose uptake and energy metabolism in susceptible worms; approved for veterinary use only.
quick: VETERINARY: dogs commonly 50 mg/kg orally once daily for 3 (up to 5) consecutive days. NOT FDA-approved for humans
Veterinary oral granules/suspension; giving with food may improve absorption
No human indication; benzimidazoles generally avoided in early pregnancy in animals/humans
Not a human drug; no established human dosing
Hepatically metabolized to active oxfendazole; monitor in animals with liver disease
Veterinary: response to deworming, occasional GI upset; (humans) no approved monitoring framework
summary: Fenbendazole is a broad-spectrum benzimidazole anthelmintic (e.g., Panacur, Safe-Guard) approved for VETERINARY use only - it is NOT FDA-approved for humans for any indication. In animals (dogs, cats, cattle, horses, swine and others) it treats gastrointestinal nematodes including roundworms (Toxocara/Toxascaris), hookworms, whipworms, and certain tapeworms (Taenia), and is used off-label against Giardia. A common canine regimen is 50 mg/kg by mouth once daily for 3 (up to 5) consecutive days. It works by binding parasite beta-tubulin, disrupting microtubule formation and impairing the worm's glucose uptake and energy metabolism, leading to parasite death; it is selectively more toxic to parasite than to mammalian tubulin and is generally very well tolerated in animals. Despite widespread internet claims, fenbendazole has NOT been proven safe or effective as a human cancer treatment, has no approved human dose, formulation, or monitoring framework, and is unstudied in human clinical trials.
indications: VETERINARY: treatment and control of gastrointestinal nematodes in animals - roundworms (ascarids), hookworms, whipworms, and certain tapeworms (Taenia species)
VETERINARY (commonly off-label): treatment of Giardia infection in dogs
Note: NOT FDA-approved for humans; human cancer use is unproven and not recommended

dosage.d: 50 mg/kg by mouth once daily for 3 consecutive days (may extend to 5 days)
50 mg/kg by mouth once daily for 3-5 (sometimes up to 7) consecutive days
Dose per the approved label for cattle, horses, swine and other species
No FDA-approved human dose, formulation, or indication

admin: VETERINARY product - administer to animals only as directed by a veterinarian, mixed with a small amount of food
Give the full multi-day course (e.g., 3 consecutive days) to ensure efficacy; complete the course even if signs improve
Giving with food (especially a fatty meal) may improve absorption of the benzimidazole
Repeat the deworming course as recommended (e.g., follow-up courses for persistent infection)
Not for human administration; keep out of reach of children
moa: Fenbendazole is a benzimidazole anthelmintic. It binds with high affinity to the beta-tubulin subunit of the parasite's microtubules, inhibiting tubulin polymerization and the formation of microtubules. Loss of functional microtubules disrupts vital cellular processes in the worm, including the uptake of glucose, leading to depletion of glycogen and ATP and impaired energy metabolism; the parasite is immobilized and dies. The drug is selectively more active against parasite (helminth) tubulin than mammalian tubulin, which accounts for its wide margin of safety in the host. In the liver it is metabolized to the active metabolite oxfendazole (fenbendazole sulfoxide).

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to fenbendazole or other benzimidazoles (in the treated animal)
relative: Severely debilitated, sick, or very young/old animals (use under veterinary guidance)
Early pregnancy in animals (benzimidazole class caution)
Concurrent severe parasite burden where rapid die-off could cause reactions
monitor: (Humans) there is no established monitoring framework because it is not approved

preg: Not for human use. As a benzimidazole, it is generally avoided in the early part of pregnancy in animals because of theoretical embryotoxic/teratogenic concerns of the class; veterinary use in pregnant animals should follow product-specific guidance.
lact: Not for human use. Data on milk transfer are limited; veterinary use in lactating animals should follow product-specific guidance.
renal: Not a human medication; there is no established human dosing. In animals it is primarily eliminated via metabolism and feces, and dose adjustment for renal function is generally not required.
hepatic: Fenbendazole is metabolized in the liver to its active metabolite oxfendazole; in animals with significant hepatic disease, use under veterinary guidance and monitor, as metabolism may be altered.

major: No clinically significant major interactions established at usual veterinary doses
moderate: Bromsalans (salicylanilide flukicides) - concurrent use with fenbendazole has caused abortions/deaths in some species; avoid co-administration
Other benzimidazoles - overlapping mechanism; no benefit to combining
minor: May theoretically interact with drugs affecting hepatic metabolism
interactions.food: Giving with food (especially fatty food) increases absorption of the benzimidazole.
interactions.diagnostics: Not applicable to human laboratory testing.

common: Generally very well tolerated in animals
serious: Reactions from rapid death of a heavy parasite load (e.g., in massive infections)
rare: Reported rare bone marrow suppression at very high/prolonged exposures (off-label/human self-dosing context)
emergency: (Humans) effects of unsupervised self-dosing are not characterized - seek medical/poison-center advice

monitoring: Veterinary: follow-up fecal examination to confirm clearance of the parasite
Humans: there is no approved monitoring framework; use in humans is not recommended
counsel: This is a VETERINARY dewormer for animals only and is NOT approved for human use - do not take it yourself or give it to people
Give it to your pet exactly as your veterinarian directs and complete the full multi-day course, even if your pet seems better
Mixing the dose with a little food (including fatty food) helps it work; report vomiting, diarrhea, facial swelling or hives
Do not rely on internet claims that this drug treats human cancer - it has not been proven safe or effective for that and is not approved
Keep the product out of reach of children and store as directed
pk: Begins killing susceptible parasites over the multi-day course in animals
Variable, often low oral absorption; peak levels generally within several hours to a day
Relatively short for the parent drug; converted to active oxfendazole (species-dependent)
Multi-day dosing (e.g., 3 days) maintains exposure for efficacy
Store at controlled room temperature per the veterinary product label; keep out of reach of children
pearls: VETERINARY benzimidazole anthelmintic (Panacur/Safe-Guard) - NOT FDA-approved for humans; do not use in people
Common canine regimen: 50 mg/kg orally once daily for 3 (up to 5) consecutive days; effective against roundworms, hookworms, whipworms, certain tapeworms, and off-label Giardia
Works by binding parasite beta-tubulin, disrupting microtubules and parasite energy metabolism; wide safety margin in the host (active metabolite is oxfendazole)
Widespread internet claims of human cancer benefit are UNPROVEN - no human approval, no standardized dose/formulation, no clinical-trial efficacy, and no monitoring framework
Avoid co-administration with salicylanilide flukicides (bromsalans) in animals
missed: Not applicable to humans. For treated animals, give a missed dose of a multi-day course as soon as remembered and continue the remaining days; if a full day is missed, contact the veterinarian about whether to extend or repeat the course - do not double the dose.
overdose: Fenbendazole has a wide margin of safety, and overdose in animals is usually well tolerated, sometimes with mild gastrointestinal upset. There is no specific antidote; management is supportive. In humans (not an approved use), the effects of large or prolonged self-administered doses are not well characterized; seek medical or poison-control advice and provide supportive care.
